source_span: Despite the sequential pickup in August, we estimate that core PCE inflation has slowed to a 2.5% annualized pace over the last three months... This slowdown mostly reflects the waning impulses from tariff pass-through, energy pass-through, software/accessories price hikes, and portfolio [effects].
source_chain: August core PCE accelerated (+0.27% m/m, above pre-print expectations) and Middle East escalation lifted oil/product prices, which is why the Fed turned hawkish; therefore Goldman's own 3-month-annualized core PCE estimate is already down to 2.5% once tariff/energy/software pass-through effects are stripped out, and its commodity desk forecasts Brent easing to $85/bbl by December as Middle East exports recover; therefore Goldman keeps its call for just one more 25bp hike (Oct 27-28) and then a flat rate, with cuts from late 2027; the named risk that would break this is renewed escalation that destroys more energy infrastructure, not the August print itself, which GS explicitly already priced in.
pulse_chain: The Fed hiked to 3.75-4.00%, and futures price ~75bp more by next June, consistent with a historical pattern of markets underpricing hiking cycles (1994, 2022); Goldman's dissenting short-cycle call (one more hike at the Oct 27-28 meeting, then flat) 'needs the data to start cooperating'; therefore August's core PCE beat (+0.27%) plus a crude jump from strikes on Saudi infrastructure is presented as the mechanism the short-cycle case 'has no answer for', because an active energy shock feeding into the discount rate cannot be looked through; invalidation is whether the 10-year closes decisively above 5% before the October meeting, against BTIG's 4.92% level that would flip the trend.
why: The pulse asserts that Goldman's short-cycle case is undermined by an August energy/inflation shock it 'has no answer for', but Goldman's own note already incorporates that exact August core PCE print and an explicit Middle East energy-escalation risk into an unchanged one-more-hike-then-flat forecast (with oil seen easing to $85/bbl by December) — the pulse reverses the note's conclusion that this data doesn't break the case into a claim that it does.
